blocks.heading: HIV, AIDS and workplace productivity
blocks.text: Illness associated with HIV and AIDS can affect attendance, working capacity, skills continuity and household care demands, potentially disrupting output and raising replacement costs. Effects vary; HIV status alone does not establish that a person cannot work. Support, confidentiality, non-discrimination and access to appropriate prevention, care and treatment services matter. Stigma can damage cooperation and discourage seeking support. Discuss the business mechanisms conditionally rather than label all affected people unproductive. This is a workplace-impact lesson, not medical advice or a reason to exclude workers. The ILO emphasises care, support and non-discrimination in its [workplace code](https://www.ilo.org/publications/ilo-code-practice-hivaids-and-world-work).

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: A fictional workshop faces periods of illness-related absence and care demands affecting some staff; no assumption is made about any individual’s diagnosis or capability. Absences can interrupt a task sequence and create a need for cover. Cross-skilling and supportive arrangements can reduce disruption while protecting dignity; blaming or excluding people based on perceived status can worsen relationships.
